papers.title: Transient hypoparathyroidism and symptomatic hypocalcemia complicating babesiosis.
papers.abstract: Babesiosis, caused by Babesia microti, is a tick-borne intraerythrocytic infection with diverse manifestations, but endocrine complications are rarely reported. We describe a 60-year-old man who presented with fever, chills, and cognitive symptoms and was diagnosed with babesiosis by peripheral smear, serology, and polymerase chain reaction. Despite improvement with atovaquone and azithromycin, he developed confusion, paresthesia, and fatigue, prompting further investigation. Laboratory testing revealed hypocalcemia (total calcium, 6.8 mg/dL [SI: 1.7 mmol/L]; reference range, 8.4-10.4 mg/dL [SI: 2.10-2.60 mmol/L]); ionized calcium, 3.8 mg/dL (SI: 0.95 mmol/L; reference range, 4.7-5.5 mg/dL [SI: 1.17-1.37 mmol/L]), a low parathyroid hormone concentration of 9 pg/mL (SI: 9 ng/L; reference range, 18-88 pg/mL [SI: 1.9-9.3 pmol/L]), and hyperphosphatemia, with phosphate concentration of 5.7 mg/dL (SI: 1.84 mmol/L; reference range, 2.5-4.5 mg/dL [SI: 0.81-1.45 mmol/L]), consistent with hypoparathyroidism, with normal magnesium and vitamin D levels. Other etiologies were excluded. He was treated with intravenous calcium followed by oral calcium and calcitriol, resulting in symptomatic and biochemical improvement. Serial monitoring demonstrated gradual recovery of parathyroid function, allowing discontinuation of calcitriol. At follow-up, calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone normalized, and symptoms resolved. This case describes transient hypoparathyroidism associated with babesiosis, with possible cytokine- or immune-mediated mechanisms.

papers.title: Infective Endocarditis Diagnosed by 2023 Duke-ISCVID Criteria with Negative Blood Culture and 18F-FDG PET/CT Findings.
papers.abstract: A 69-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a fever suggestive of infective endocarditis. His medical history included mitral valve replacement and tricuspid valve repair. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed no definite vegetations, and 18Fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18FDG-PET/CT) showed no abnormal cardiac uptake. His blood culture results were negative. Finally, the patient was diagnosed with Bartonella-associated infective endocarditis, with markedly elevated IgG titers against Bartonella henselae (≥1: 1,024). Bartonella endocarditis should be considered in patients with negative blood culture and 18FDG-PET/CT findings.

papers.title: Diseases causing nervous signs in cattle in South America.
papers.abstract: Neurological diseases in cattle are among the most important diagnostic challenges in veterinary practice and diagnostic laboratories. In South America, surveillance systems and diagnostic networks have progressively expanded the recognition of diseases causing nervous signs in cattle, yet available information remains fragmented across countries. This review integrates current knowledge on the main diseases causing nervous signs in cattle in South America, with emphasis on their clinical presentation, etiopathogenesis, pathology, and diagnostic relevance, and includes brief information on treatment, control, and prevention. For practical purposes, bovine neurologic disorders are organized according to their etiologic origin into infectious, parasitic, toxic, metabolic, neoplastic, and genetic or congenital. Among infectious conditions, rabies remains the most important viral encephalitis in the region, while bovine herpesviral meningoencephalitis, malignant catarrhal fever, listeriosis, thrombotic meningoencephalitis, and suppurative bacterial infections are also relevant differential diagnoses. Parasitic disorders such as cerebral babesiosis, Trypanosoma vivax infection, nervous coccidiosis, neosporosis, coenurosis, and amoebic meningoencephalitis are less frequent but regionally significant. Toxic and metabolic causes are highly diverse and include plant and fungal intoxications, pesticide and lead poisoning, polioencephalomalacia, hypomagnesemia, vitamin A deficiency, ketosis/fatty liver syndrome, and hypocalcemia. Less common but clinically important conditions include nervous system neoplasms and congenital or hereditary disorders. A single integrated table summarizes, for each condition, the etiologic agent, geographic distribution, affected age group and neurolocalization, main neurological syndrome, principal lesions, field diagnostic aids, samples for laboratory confirmation, laboratory diagnostic methods, and the available treatment and control measures. This review highlights the wide etiologic spectrum of bovine diseases causing nervous signs in South America and emphasizes the importance of a systematic diagnostic approach integrating epidemiology, clinical neurology, gross pathology, histopathology, and targeted ancillary tests. A better understanding of these conditions should improve differential diagnosis, therapeutic decision-making, surveillance, and preventive strategies in cattle production systems across the region.

papers.title: Lyme Carditis: Cardiac Inflammation, Proposed Molecular Mimicry, Diagnosis, and Management.
papers.abstract: Lyme disease is an important tick-borne infection in North America, Europe, and parts of Asia. Although cardiac involvement is uncommon, it can have serious clinical consequences. Atrioventricular (AV) block is the most characteristic manifestation of Lyme carditis. Cardiac tissue infection and local inflammatory responses are implicated in its pathogenesis, whereas molecular mimicry and antigenic cross-reactivity remain proposed mechanisms whose contribution to human cardiac injury has not been established. AV conduction can deteriorate rapidly, and some patients develop high-grade or complete AV block. Continuous electrocardiographic monitoring is therefore important, and temporary pacing should be provided when clinically indicated. Because conduction abnormalities often improve with appropriate antimicrobial therapy, permanent pacemaker implantation is generally deferred unless clinically necessary. Diagnosis requires an integrated assessment of epidemiological exposure, clinical manifestations, serological results, electrocardiographic findings, echocardiographic findings, and alternative etiologies. When clinical suspicion is high, antimicrobial therapy should be initiated promptly to reduce the risk of complications. Most patients experience substantial or complete recovery of AV conduction after appropriate treatment.

papers.title: A novel 17-plex multi-pathogen detection for rapid and accurate diagnosis of tick-borne diseases.
papers.abstract: In recent years, anthropogenic ecological disruption has escalated tick-borne zoonoses; ticks transmit taxonomically diverse pathogens with overlapping clinical signs, challenging precise diagnosis and increasing risk of simultaneous detection in pooled samples. Despite advancements, current sequencing technologies, such as Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS), Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) assays, and antibody-based detection methods, are hampered by limitations including extended processing times and limited detection throughput. These constraints significantly hinder their effectiveness in high-throughput pathogen screening for animal or patient samples. To address these challenges, we developed an innovative multi-detection method based on the Multi-analyte Suspension Assay (MASA), enabling rapid and accurate diagnosis of a comprehensive panel of 17 vector-borne pathogens. This 17-plex panel comprises Rickettsia spp., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Borrelia recurrentis, Babesia spp., Borrelia burgdorferi, Rickettsia prowazekii, Rickettsia heilongjiangensis, Orientia tsutsugamushi, Coxiella burnetii, Leptospira, Bartonella spp., Candidatus Ehrlichia erytraense, Hantaan Virus (HTNV), Seoul Virus (SEOV), Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV), Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome Virus (SFTSV), and Tick-Borne Encephalitis Virus (TBEV). By combining this novel method with traditional techniques, including nested PCR and Real-Time Quantitative Reverse Transcription PCR (qRT-PCR), we achieved accurate detection of pathogens such as Rickettsia spp., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, and SFTSV in tick samples. Notably, the technique revealed the co-existence of multiple pathogens within the same sample group, highlighting its ability in identifying co-detection of pathogens. Additionally, in suspected cases of tick-borne pathogen infection in febrile patients, the method quickly identified positive results for SFTSV and Rickettsia spp. These preliminary results suggest the potential of this method as a promising screening tool for clinical diagnostics, although larger-scale validation is warranted. This method provides a preliminary technical candidate approach for the development of more sensitive field-deployable detection tools.

papers.title: Molecular evidence of vector/blood borne and hemotropic bacteria in dogs and cats from El Salvador, Central America.
papers.abstract: Latin America's high biodiversity, together with socioeconomic and ecological conditions, favors the persistence of vectors and vector-borne bacterial pathogens in domestic animals. Data on vector-borne pathogens in domestic dogs and cats in Central America remain limited, and reports from El Salvador are scarce. This study aimed to investigate the occurrence of Bartonella spp., Anaplasma spp., Ehrlichia spp., and hemotropic Mycoplasma spp. in domestic dogs and cats from the metropolitan area of San Salvador, El Salvador. For this purpose, blood samples were collected from 269 dogs and 59 cats in veterinary clinics. Four feline (6.78%; 95% CI: 2.67-16.18%) and one canine (0.37%; 95% CI: 0.07-2.08%) samples were positive for Bartonella spp. by a quantitative real-time TaqMan based PCR (qPCR) based on the NADH dehydrogenase gamma subunit (nuoG) gene. In a TaqMan-based multiplex qPCR targeting the gene encoding the 60-kDa heat shock protein (groEL gene), whereas 19 canine (7.06%; 95% CI: 4.57-10.77%) and our feline (6.78%; 95% CI: 2.67-16.18%) samples were positive for Ehrlichia spp., eight canine (2.97%; 95% CI: 1.51-5.76%) and one feline (1.69%; 95% CI: 0.30-9.00%) samples were positive for Anaplasma spp. Five feline (8.47%; 95% CI: 3.67-18.35%) and three canine (1.12%; 95% CI: 0.38-3.23%) samples were positive in a SYBRGreen-based qPCR targeting the 16 S rRNA gene of hemotropic Mycoplasma spp. Sequencing and phylogenetic analyses allowed the identification of Bartonella henselae in four (one dog and three cat samples) of the five Bartonella-positive animals, and 'Candidatus Mycoplasma haemominutum' in three out of five hemoplasma-positive cats analyzed. In dogs, hemoplasma species could not be determined due to the lack of sequencing data. The Anaplasma spp. and Ehrlichia spp. positive samples did not yield amplicons in the conventional PCR assays for sequencing, precluding molecular identification at the species level. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first molecular detection of Bartonella spp. and hemoplasmas in domestic dogs and cats from El Salvador and the first molecular evidence of Anaplasma spp. and Ehrlichia spp. in domestic cats in the country.

papers.title: Prevalence of Powassan Virus Infection in Children with Suspected Lyme Disease.
papers.abstract: Both Lyme disease and Powassan virus (POWV) are transmitted by the bite of the Ixodes tick. While severe POWV encephalitis cases are uncommon in children, milder infections may be underdiagnosed. We performed a case-control study nested within a prospective cohort of children < 21 years evaluated for Lyme disease at one of eight Pedi Lyme Net emergency departments. We selected children with early or early-disseminated Lyme disease (n=305) with age, sex, center and symptom matched clinical mimics (n=295). Using biobanked research specimens, we performed POWV two-tier serology with confirmatory focus neutralization testing (FNT) and a reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) test. We defined a POWV infection with a positive two-tier serology or RT-PCR test. We compared the prevalence of POWV between children with Lyme disease and matched mimics. Of the 600 included children, the median age was 9 years (interquartile range 6-14 years) and 377 (63%) were male. POWV infection was more common in the children with Lyme disease (8.5%, 95% confidence interval (CI) 5.4-11.7%) compared to matched mimics (0.7%, 95% CI 0.1-2.4%; difference 7.9%, 95% CI 4.6-11.1; adjusted odds ratio 5.0, 95% CI 1.2-21.9). Of the 28 children with a positive POWV two-tier serology test, 11 (39%) had a positive FNT test. None of the RT-PCR tests were positive (0%, 95% CI 0-0.7%). A substantial minority of children with Lyme disease had serologic evidence of POWV co-infection compared with matched clinical mimics. Clinically unrecognized POWV infections were more common than previously acknowledged.

papers.title: Molecular detection and therapeutic management of Babesia gibsoni and Ehrlichia canis co-infection in dogs along with characterization of the pathogens.
papers.abstract: Tick-borne hemoparasitic infections constitute an important cause of clinical morbidity in dogs, particularly in endemic regions where vector exposure facilitates concurrent transmission of multiple pathogens. This study aimed to molecularly detect and characterize Babesia gibsoni and Ehrlichia canis co-infection in dogs, assess associated clinico-hemato-biochemical alterations, and evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of artesunate-atovaquone-doxycycline (AAD) regimen. A total of 184 clinically suspected dogs were screened by internally controlled multiplex PCR, and positive cases were further confirmed by species-specific real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) and sequencing. The prevalence of B. gibsoni and E. canis co-infection was 7.6% (14/184). Eight infected dogs were treated with AAD protocol and the relative abundance of parasite target DNA was assessed on days 0, 10, 28, and 90 using relative quantification (RQ) qPCR targeting B. gibsoni 18S rRNA and E. canis VirB9 gene that has been normalized to canine β-actin by the 2-ΔΔCt method. Infected dogs exhibited normocytic-normochromic anemia, thrombocytopenia, hypoproteinaemia, hyperglobulinaemia, hyperbilirubinemia, azotaemia, high serum alkaline phosphatase and aspartate transaminase level whereas, mean creatinine level were found within normal physiological range. Following AAD therapy, dogs showed rapid clinical recovery, with significant improvement in hemato-biochemical parameters by day 90. Significant reduction in parasite DNA load was noted, reflected by rising Ct values and progressively declining log RQ values for both pathogens. These findings indicated that the AAD regimen showed potential effectiveness against canine B. gibsoni and E. canis co-infection, however this preliminary clinical observation may be validated through further controlled trials.

papers.title: Current Status and Epidemiologic Perspectives on Mite-, Flea-, and Louse-Borne Diseases in Korea.
papers.abstract: This narrative review summarizes the epidemiology and public health relevance of mite-, flea-, and louse-borne infections in Korea. We combined English- and Korean-language literature with national surveillance data. Annual and monthly notifications of scrub typhus and murine typhus were summarized for 2001-2024, and mean annual regional incidence was assessed for 2015-2024 using population statistics. National surveillance recorded 149,303 scrub typhus cases and 660 murine typhus cases during 2001-2024. Scrub typhus showed a pronounced autumn peak and higher incidence in southern and southwestern regions. Murine typhus showed a recent increase in annual case notifications, reaching 60 cases in 2024, with heterogeneous regional patterns. Bartonella henselae infection has been documented in Korea, but its burden remains uncertain. Epidemic typhus and louse-borne relapsing fever have not been officially reported for several decades, although reemergence in vulnerable populations remains possible. Mite-, flea-, and louse-borne infections remain neglected components of the febrile illness landscape in Korea. Improved diagnostic awareness, strengthened surveillance, and continued collaboration are needed to better define their burden and to detect potential reemergence.

papers.title: Rickettsial Pathogens and Piroplasms Detected in Ticks Collected from Domestic Mammals in the Urabá Region, Colombia.
papers.abstract: Ticks transmit a wide range of pathogens of veterinary and public health importance, yet information on tick-borne agents in the Urabá region of Colombia remains scarce. A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted in nine municipalities of Urabá, Antioquia, encompassing dispersed rural areas, Indigenous communities, peri-urban areas, and urban centers. Ticks collected from cattle, equids, dogs, and pigs were morphologically identified and grouped into 139 homogeneous pools (901 ticks), which were screened by multiplex and conventional PCR for Rickettsia spp., Anaplasma spp., Ehrlichia spp., and piroplasms (Babesia spp./Theileria spp.); positive amplicons were sequenced, and phylogenetic analyses were performed for Rickettsia spp. and piroplasms. Overall, 35 pools (25.18%) were positive for at least one agent. Ehrlichia spp. showed the highest minimum infection rate (MIR; 18.87 per 1000 ticks), followed by Anaplasma spp. (8.88), Rickettsia spp. (6.66 by the multiplex assay and 8.88 by gltA amplification), and piroplasms (6.66). Rickettsia spp. sequences clustered within the spotted fever group, Anaplasma spp. sequences were identical to several members of the A. marginale group, and the piroplasm sequence clustered within Theileria equi genotype C, representing the first molecular report of this parasite in the region. Dermacentor nitens and Rhipicephalus microplus were positive for all agents evaluated. These findings provide molecular evidence of tick-borne agents of veterinary and potential zoonotic importance in Urabá and support the strengthening of surveillance under a One Health approach.

papers.title: Tafenoquine-associated serum redox metabolic remodeling during Babesia microti infection in mice.
papers.abstract: Babesiosis is an important tick-borne parasitic disease with limited therapeutic options. Tafenoquine exhibits potent antibabesial activity, but the metabolic basis underlying its antibabesial activity remains unclear. Here, we investigated metabolic alterations associated with tafenoquine treatment during Babesia microti infection, with a focus on redox regulation. BALB/c mice infected with B. microti were treated with tafenoquine, and serum metabolites were profiled using widely targeted metabolomics. Differential metabolic changes were identified by multivariate and univariate analyses, and redox-related alterations were further evaluated together with biochemical measurements of antioxidant defense and oxidative damage markers. Serum metabolic profiles differed between tafenoquine-treated and untreated infected mice, particularly during the acute infection stage. Redox-related metabolic remodeling was characterized by alterations in metabolites involved in cysteine and methionine metabolism, glutathione metabolism, taurine and related metabolism, and the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Following tafenoquine treatment, superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase activities in serum were lower, whereas malondialdehyde levels were higher, consistent with lipid peroxidation. Together, these metabolomic and biochemical findings are consistent with substantial redox metabolic remodeling associated with tafenoquine treatment during B. microti infection.

papers.title: CRISPR-cas systems in protozoan parasites: Genome editing, functional genomics, gene regulation and emerging applications.
papers.abstract: Protozoan parasites possess complex genomes, unusual DNA-repair mechanisms, multiple developmental stages, and, in several species, intracellular or vector-dependent life cycles that complicate functional genetic studies. CRISPR-Cas9 has become a central tool for functional genomics in these organisms, enabling targeted gene disruption, replacement, tagging, nucleotide modification and genome-wide functional screening. However, editing efficiency and outcomes vary substantially among parasite species and depend not only on Cas9-mediated double-strand break formation but also on target accessibility, guide design, delivery method, parasite stage, DNA-repair capacity, donor availability, selection and the biological cost of the induced lesion. This review focuses primarily on experimentally established Cas9-mediated genome editing in Plasmodium, Leishmania, Toxoplasma gondii, Trypanosoma, Babesia, Theileria and Cryptosporidium. We compare plasmid-based and transient expression, ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, electroporation/nucleofection, stage-specific delivery, guide and donor design, selection strategies, editing outcomes, and molecular and functional validation. Particular emphasis is placed on homology-directed repair (HDR), canonical non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ) and single-strand annealing (SSA), which determine whether editing results in indels, precise sequence replacement, tagging or larger genomic deletions. Species-specific differences are illustrated by efficient NHEJ-mediated disruption in Toxoplasma, donor-dependent repair in Plasmodium and Cryptosporidium, SSA-associated repair in Leishmania, efficient homologous recombination in trypanosomatids, precise editing in Babesia, and stage-specific delivery constraints in Theileria. The review further examines the progression from single-gene editing to marker-free manipulation, base editing, conditional approaches and genome-wide functional screens. Cas12a, CRISPRi/a, prime editing and related systems are discussed as emerging extensions. Overall, this repair- and delivery-centred framework explains why CRISPR editing differs among protozoan parasites and identifies the experimentally validated limitations that currently shape their genome-engineering potential.

papers.title: Trends in Lyme disease incidence in England, 2013 to 2024.
papers.abstract: Official Lyme disease incidence figures for England are based on the number of cases with a laboratory-confirmed diagnosis from the national reference laboratory. However, these figures underestimate the true incidence of acute cases since patients can also be diagnosed clinically without the need for laboratory testing. The use of a multiplication factor has been proposed to estimate total Lyme disease incidence from the number of laboratory-confirmed cases. The current multiplication factor is derived from data spanning 1998-2016 and is thought to be outdated, in part due to the introduction of new national Lyme disease management guidance in 2018. The aim of this study was to analyse more recent laboratory and primary care data to identify trends in case numbers and to derive updated estimates of the total annual number of acute Lyme disease cases in England. Data spanning 2013-2024 from the national reference laboratory and a primary care data source were analysed using seasonal time series models. The presence of structural breaks was investigated using the PELT or BinSeg methods, and annual multiplication factors were estimated using a Poisson regression model. No substantial change was found in the number of laboratory-confirmed Lyme cases from 2013 to 2024 in England, whereas the number of cases diagnosed in primary care increased significantly over the same period, with an average of an additional 498 cases per year. This has increased our best estimate of the multiplication factor from 2.35 (95% confidence interval, 1.81-2.88) to 6.20 (6.17-6.24), which is the average for the years 2020-2024. Use of this updated multiplication factor should improve the accuracy of annual symptomatic Lyme disease case estimates for England.

papers.title: Spatial and Temporal Patterns of Blacklegged Tick (Ixodes scapularis) Populations and Lyme Disease Cases in Ontario, Canada, From 2007 to 2019.
papers.abstract: Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi sensu stricto, is a growing human and animal health concern in Canada due to the rapid range expansion of its vector, the blacklegged tick (Ixodes scapularis). Various forms of surveillance have been performed for Lyme disease in Ontario, including mandatory human case reporting, passive tick surveillance (tick submissions from the public), active tick surveillance (tick dragging), and canine seroprevalence (proprietary data). This study assessed and compared the temporal trends, seasonality, and spatial distribution of blacklegged ticks and Lyme disease in Ontario using data from four types of surveillance. Time series analysis was applied to visualize temporal trends, followed by a generalized linear auto-regressive moving average modelling approach to assess the trend and seasonal effects. Human Lyme disease incidence per 100,000, passive I. scapularis submission rate per 100,000, B. burgdorferi prevalence in I. scapularis from active surveillance, and canine B. burgdorferi seroprevalence were spatially displayed at the public health unit level. An increasing trend in human cases, I. scapularis collected via passive and active approaches, and canine seropositivity were observed over time. Ixodes scapularis counts from passive and active surveillance peaked in May and October. Human cases peaked in July, while canine seroprevalence peaked in May. Human case incidence, tick submission rate, B. burgdorferi infection prevalence in I. scapularis from active surveillance, and canine seroprevalence were highest in public health units in eastern Ontario, but this was not consistent from year to year. This study demonstrates a significant disparity in Ontario's yearly, seasonal, and spatial patterns of I. scapularis, human Lyme disease cases, and canine seropositivity, challenging the comparability of risk across regions. A One Health surveillance approach that systematically collects and integrates animal, human, and environmental data at finer spatial and temporal scales is proposed.

papers.title: Vector-Borne Infections, PANS, and Autoimmune Encephalitis: A Series of Five Cases.
papers.abstract: Autoimmune encephalitis is increasingly recognized as a central mechanism underlying many infection-associated neuropsychiatric syndromes. Pediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome (PANS), a subset of autoimmune encephalitis, is defined as the abrupt onset of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and/or severe food restriction accompanied by concurrent mood, behavioral, and cognitive disturbances. In this case series, five pediatric patients developed clinical features consistent with autoimmune encephalitis and PANS following infection with vector-borne pathogens. These cases illustrate that vector-borne infections are frequently polymicrobial and can precipitate significant neuropsychiatric symptoms, including severe mood dysregulation and thought disturbances. When children and adolescents present with neuropsychiatric symptoms, clinicians should consider vector-borne infectious etiologies in the differential diagnosis.

papers.title: Structural ICD-10 coding gaps and economic burden of underrecognized chronic conditions: a machine learning analysis of MEPS 2019-2022 and CDC PLACES.
papers.abstract: To quantify the economic burden of chronic and invisible illness using federal open data, document structural ICD-10 coding gaps, and evaluate machine learning (ML) performance for individual-level healthcare expenditure prediction. We analyzed four consecutive MEPS waves (2019-2022; n = 17,909-22,552 adults/year) with the 2024 CDC PLACES dataset (45 states). Outcomes included total annual expenditure, out-of-pocket costs, and work-loss days. ICD-10-CM codes in MEPS Medical Conditions files were searched for invisible illness coverage. XGBoost and Random Forest predicted log-transformed expenditure from 14 features; ordinary least squares (OLS) served as baseline. Geographic burden was scored using nine composite CDC PLACES indicators. Adults with ≥1 chronic condition incurred 3.3 times higher mean annual expenditures and 80% more work-loss days. Autoimmune patients faced the highest costs ($24,148-$26,630/year): 3.0-3.7× higher than adults without that specific condition, and 5.8-7.6× higher than adults with no chronic condition at all. Because the MEPS public-use file reports ICD-10-CM diagnoses only as 3-character categories, we re-ran the search at that granularity: Lyme disease remained at zero records across all four years, and long COVID in every year its code existed, but the categories containing fibromyalgia and ME-CFS were not uniformly zero and cannot be attributed to these two conditions specifically. XGBoost achieved R2 = 0.30-0.32 under cross-validation, a 13-17% improvement over OLS; activity limitation was the dominant predictor. Southern states ranked highest on composite burden; disability and uninsured rates were positively correlated across the 43 states with complete indicator data (r = 0.37, p = 0.014). Lyme disease and long COVID show a genuine structural coding gap in MEPS; fibromyalgia and ME-CFS could not be confirmed present or absent, because the file merges their codes with unrelated diagnoses. ML improves expenditure prediction but cannot compensate for upstream data gaps. High disease burden co-occurring with low insurance coverage in Southern states demands targeted policy responses. Federal open data fail to capture Lyme disease and long COVID; their coding granularity cannot resolve fibromyalgia or ME-CFS from broader categories. Reforms in ICD coding, survey design, and data linkage are needed to make these populations visible to health policy and service planning.

papers.title: Participant-Reported Use of Human-Encountered Tick-Testing Results in Healthcare Settings: A Cross-sectional Survey.
papers.abstract: The rising incidence and expanding geographic distribution of tick-borne diseases in the United States have led to innovative approaches to surveillance and risk assessment. Human-encountered tick-testing programs provide submitters with tick identification and pathogen-screening results, although clinical guidelines advise against using tick pathogen results to direct patient management. We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 11 936 individuals who submitted ticks to the SUNY Upstate Tick Testing Program during 2019-2021. Of 2576 respondents (22.6%), 2560 answered the healthcare-use question; 824 (32.2%) reported using the result when seeking medical help. Among these respondents, 398 reported that a healthcare provider performed diagnostic testing, and 476 perceived that medication was prescribed based on the tick-testing result. Because the survey relied on participant self-report and did not capture symptoms, timing, medication type, clinical indication, or provider rationale, it cannot determine whether tick-testing results caused or improved clinical decisions. The findings nevertheless indicate that respondents bring these results into healthcare interactions. Communication accompanying tick-testing reports should emphasize that detection in a submitted tick does not establish human infection and that such results should not replace established clinical assessment or diagnostic testing.

papers.title: First molecular detection of Ehrlichia spp. and Theileria spp. closely related to Theileria parva in Hyalomma dromedarii ticks infesting camels in the United Arab Emirates.
papers.abstract: Tick-borne pathogens pose a growing threat to animal health and livestock production, particularly in arid regions where Hyalomma ticks are abundant. Hyalomma dromedarii, the predominant camel tick in the Middle East and North Africa, has been implicated in the transmission of several bacterial and protozoal pathogens. Despite the economic importance of camels in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), comprehensive surveillance of tick-borne microorganisms in H. dromedarii across the country remains limited. This study investigated the occurrence of Anaplasma, Rickettsia, Ehrlichia, Theileria, and Babesia in H. dromedarii collected from camels in the UAE and characterized the detected pathogens using molecular and phylogenetic analyses. A total of 804 camels from 182 farms in Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, and Umm Al Quwain were examined between June 2022 and October 2023. One semi-engorged female H. dromedarii tick was selected from each camel whenever available, yielding 671 ticks for molecular analysis. Genomic DNA was extracted and screened using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays targeting Anaplasma, Rickettsia, Ehrlichia, Theileria, and Babesia. Positive amplicons were confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and phylogenetic analyses were performed to determine their genetic relationships with previously reported isolates. No evidence of Anaplasma, Rickettsia, or Babesia DNA was detected in the analyzed ticks. In contrast, Theileria and Ehrlichia DNA were detected in 0.60% (4/671) and 0.30% (2/671) of samples, respectively. The detected Ehrlichia represents the first molecular record of this genus in H. dromedarii from the UAE. One Theileria sequence exhibited 98.96% nucleotide similarity to Theileria parva; however, species-specific PCR failed to confirm T. parva, indicating that the detected organism was a closely related Theileria species rather than confirmed T. parva. Phylogenetic analyses showed that the detected Ehrlichia and Theileria sequences clustered with corresponding reference sequences reported previously from other geographical regions. This study provides the first molecular evidence of Ehrlichia in H. dromedarii ticks in the UAE and identifies a Theileria isolate closely related to T. parva. Although pathogen prevalence was low, these findings expand current knowledge of tick-borne microorganisms associated with camel ticks in the UAE and highlight the need for continued molecular surveillance to clarify the epidemiological significance, host-pathogen interactions, and potential veterinary and One Health implications of these microorganisms in the region.

papers.title: Diversity of Ectoparasites and Vector-Borne Pathogens in Wild Carnivores: Evidence from Three Regions of Serbia.
papers.abstract: Wild carnivores can maintain ectoparasites and vector-borne pathogens at wildlife-domestic animal-human interfaces. We characterized ectoparasites and selected vector-associated agents in golden jackals (Canis aureus), red foxes (Vulpes vulpes), Eurasian badgers (Meles meles) and European wildcats (Felis silvestris) sampled in three regions of Serbia from October 2022 to January 2023. Of 122 animals examined, 77 carried ectoparasites; 68 ticks and 254 fleas were collected. Ticks comprised Ixodes ricinus (n = 37, from which n = 23 on C. aureus, n = 14 on V. vulpes), Dermacentor reticulatus (n = 23, from which n = 12 on C. aureus, n = 11 on V. vulpes), Rhipicephalus spp. (n = 3, from which n = 2 on C. aureus, n = 1 on V.vulpes), and Haemaphysalis punctata (n= 5, from which n = 2 on C. aureus, n = 3 on V.vulpes), whereas fleas comprised Ctenocephalides canis (n = 171, from which n = 97 on C. aureus, n = 64 on V. vulpes, n = 9 on Meles meles, n = 1 on Felis silvestris), C. felis (n = 36, from which n = 14 on C. aureus, n = 12 on V. vulpes, n = 10 on Meles meles), Pulex irritans (n = 25, from which n = 15 on C. aureus, n = 6 on V. vulpes, n = 4 on Meles meles), Ceratophyllus gallinae (n = 21, from which n = 5 on C. aureus, n = 16 on V. vulpes) and Xenopsylla cheopis (n = 1 on C. aureus). Molecular screening detected Hepatozoon canis DNA in six tick samples, Babesia spp. DNA in three tick preparations and Bartonella spp. DNA in 13 flea samples; the remaining bacterial, protozoal and viral targets were not detected. Sanger sequencing yielded sequences assigned to Babesia canis (n = 2), H. canis (n = 4) and Bartonella rochalimae (n = 13). Phylogenetic analyses placed the study sequences with related Eurasian reference lineages. These findings document a diverse ectoparasite fauna and vector-associated pathogen circulation in Serbian wild carnivores and support continued One Health surveillance using paired host-vector sampling.

papers.title: Tetracycline Exposure Disrupts Gut Microbiota and Immune-Antioxidant Homeostasis in Honey Bees.
papers.abstract: Antibiotic exposure can perturb the gut microbiota of honey bees, but its associations with host physiological responses remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the effects of tetracycline exposure on survival, locomotor activity, gut bacterial communities, and immune- and antioxidant-related gene expression in Apis mellifera workers maintained under controlled laboratory cage conditions. Tetracycline exposure at 100, 300, and 450 μg/mL reduced worker survival in a concentration-dependent manner, while 100 μg/mL increased daytime locomotor activity without affecting sucrose consumption. Tetracycline also altered gut bacterial community structure, with marked reductions in several core taxa, particularly Snodgrassella and Bartonella, whereas Commensalibacter, Lactobacillus Firm4 and Firm5 increased, especially at the highest concentration. Changes in immune- and antioxidant-related gene expression were more pronounced in the gut than in the head. Moreover, Snodgrassella abundance was positively correlated with Relish expression in the head and with Apidaecin and CAT expression in the gut. These findings demonstrate that tetracycline exposure reduces honey bee survival and is associated with coordinated alterations in gut bacterial communities and host physiological responses.

papers.title: An iterative subseasonal-to-interannual ecological forecast system for Ixodes scapularis, the vector of Lyme disease.
papers.abstract: Forecasting the population dynamics of disease vectors is critical for mitigating the risks of vector-borne diseases under a changing climate. We evaluate an iterative Bayesian forecast model of black-legged tick (Ixodes scapularis) phenology and population dynamics at near-term to interannual (e.g., 12-month) scales. The black-legged tick is the vector of Borrelia burgdorferi, the causative agent of human Lyme disease. Our forecasts outperformed a seasonal null model during peak questing periods when disease risk is highest. The null model was based on historical day-of-year averages. Iterative data assimilation improved forecast performance over time, demonstrating the ability to adaptively learn about climate-driven shifts in demographic parameters, and reinforcing the value of long-term data to support management. Weather and climate variables emerged as the dominant predictors of nymph survival and questing activity, with daily maximum temperature displacing humidity as the strongest predictor as the iterative forecast cycle evolved over time. Short-term forecasts driven by local weather observations were more accurate than those relying on seasonal climate forecasts, highlighting the importance of fine-scale weather dynamics and data for subannual predictions. At interannual scales, seasonal climate forecasts and vertebrate host (mouse) abundance were important for maintaining strong predictive skill in forecasting nymphal tick abundance, which is often used as a proxy for risk of human exposure to tick-borne disease (TBD), but forecasts were largely unaffected by larval abundance. Investment in monitoring efforts should prioritize observations of the nymphal stage to reduce forecast uncertainty. These results offer a path forward for operationalizing ecological forecasts of tick populations under environmental change and underscore the importance of adaptive, process-based models for managing TBD risk in a changing climate.
papers.journal: Ecological applications : a publication of the Ecological Society of America

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: This study aimed to identify diagnostically relevant antigens of Babesia bigemina using an integrative approach that combines in silico analysis and experimental validation. Candidate antigens were selected based on species specificity, predicted secretion signals, transcriptional activity, and B-cell epitopes. Selected genes were expressed in Escherichia coli, and antigenicity was evaluated by Western blot and ELISA using plasma from infected and uninfected cattle. A truncated AMA-1 fragment demonstrated strong immunoreactivity and clear discrimination between positive and negative samples. A candidate protein (BBBOND_0404230), identified through in silico screening, also showed specific immunoreactivity, but with greater variability in ELISA response. AMA-1 represents a reliable diagnostic antigen, while BBBOND_0404230 is a promising complementary marker. The combined use of these antigens may improve the performance of serological assays for bovine babesiosis.
papers.journal: Journal of advanced veterinary and animal research

papers.title: Prevalence of Bartonella spp., Borrelia spp., and piroplasmid in HIV-infected symptomatic individuals in Brazil: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Bartonella spp., Borrelia spp., and piroplasmid are increasingly recognized as vector-borne pathogens worldwide, with documented circulation in arthropod vectors and animal reservoirs in Brazil. The purpose of this study was to assess whether Bartonella exposure and/or infection were associated with specific clinical and epidemiological characteristics in HIV-infected symptomatic patients living in Brazil. The second aim was to determine if infection with a piroplasmid or Borrelia species might be detected in these patients. Epidemiological and medical history were collected for each of 75 HIV-positive participants. In a blinded manner, we assessed the presence of anti-Bartonella antibodies by indirect immunofluorescence assays (IFA) using B. henselae, B. koehlerae, B. quintana, and B. vinsonii berkhoffii (genotypes I and II) as antigens. A cut-off dilution of 1:64 was selected as a seroreactivity titer. We evaluated infection by amplifying Bartonella spp., Borrelia spp., and piroplasmid DNA from blood using quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and digital PCR (dPCR). qPCR was performed before and after BAPGM (Bartonella alpha-Proteobacteria Growth Medium)-enriched blood culture for up to 28 days, and statistical analyses were conducted in an exploratory framework. Seroreactivity to at least one Bartonella antigen was found in 47/75 (62.7%) participants. The most frequent seroreactive species were B. henselae (57.3%), and B. vinsonii subsp. berkhoffii genotype II (44.0%). Bartonella seroreactivity was associated with systemic manifestations (11/47 seroreactive vs. 1/28 non-seroreactive patients; OR = 8.25, 95% CI 1.00-68.2; p = 0.026). All participants were negative for Bartonella and Borrelia spp. qPCR and dPCR. Two participants had a low positive partition number by piroplasmid dPCR, which was not repeatable by retesting. In this cohort of HIV-infected symptomatic patients, exposure to Bartonella species was frequent, but molecular evidence confirmed by sequence analysis of Bartonella, Borrelia, and piroplasmid infection was not found. The clinical relevance of Bartonella seroreactivity remains to be clarified.

papers.title: Choroidal thickness in Bartonella henselae multifocal retinitis.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the choroid in multifocal retinitis assoiciated with Bartonella henselae infection. Other posterior uveitis diseases, such as toxoplasmosis, tend to present with a thickened choroid, and we aimed to evaluate whether this is the case in these patients as well. Consecutive cases of Bartonella henselae multifocal retinitis at Meir Medical Center in Kfar Saba, Israel, between January 2023 and December 2025 were reviewed retrospectively. The choroid in cases of retinitis was evaluated using OCT with enhanced depth imaging (EDI). Five patients (ten eyes) were included. All cases had a typical bilateral multifocal retinitis with small or mid-sized superficial retinal infiltrates. All were immunocompetent with a negative uveitis workup, including syphilis and rickettsia, but a positive Bartonella serology. All cases had a thickened choroid, which was either diffuse or focal, localized posterior to retinal infiltrates. The more involved eye of the same patient, with more inflammatory signs, also had a thicker choroid. The choroid became thinner after treatment. The choroid of patients with Bartonella henselae retinitis may be thickened as a result of the infection.
papers.journal: International journal of retina and vitreous

papers.title: Opportunistic infections mimicking post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder in transplant recipients: a scoping review of reported cases.
papers.abstract: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) is a serious complication of solid organ and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Opportunistic infections may closely resemble PTLD clinically, radiologically, or histopathologically, creating a diagnostic uncertainty potentially leading to inappropriate clinical management. This scoping review synthesizes published cases of opportunistic infections initially suspected to represent PTLD to characterize their presentation, diagnostic pitfalls, and clinical outcomes. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we searched PubMed, PubMed Central, and EMBASE through September 30, 2025, for reports of opportunistic infections initially suspected as PTLD in transplant recipients. Data on patient demographics, transplant characteristics, pathogens, clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, management, and outcomes were extracted and summarized descriptively. Thirty-five studies reporting 37 individual cases met the inclusion criteria. Most patients were solid organ transplant recipients (97%), with kidney transplantation predominating. The median age of patients was 44.5 years, and the median interval from transplantation to clinical presentation was 48 months. Bacterial infections were the most common (51%), led by Bartonella henselae, followed by fungal (27%), parasitic (14%), and viral (8%) infections. Radiological mimicry was the predominant mechanism leading to suspicion of PTLD, whereas histopathological examination ultimately established the correct diagnosis in most cases. Tissue biopsy, combined with pathogen-specific microbiological or molecular testing, was central for the diagnosis. Diagnostic delays resulted in inappropriate PTLD-directed therapy in several patients and were associated with severe complications, including graft dysfunction and death. Opportunistic infections represent important mimics of PTLD across a broad range of pathogens and organ systems. Because imaging findings and EBV-associated laboratory abnormalities lack specificity, early tissue diagnosis integrated with microbiological and molecular investigations is essential before initiating PTLD-directed therapy. Greater awareness of these infectious mimics may reduce diagnostic error, preserve graft function and improve outcomes in transplant recipients. Not applicable.
